feedback: If a learner says a day is 12 hours because 'the clock stops at 12', have them watch/track the second lap explicitly, naming the pm hours on the first lap (midday to midnight) and then the am hours on the second lap (midnight to midday), so they see the 12 numbers reused.
If they reach 24 but can't explain it, ask them to point to where the first 12 hours end and the second 12 begin on the day-strip.
Reinforce by matching times across the 12-hour and 24-hour clocks (1pm = 13:00) so the double sweep is anchored to a familiar format.
activities.intendedInsight: A whole day is 24 hours because the hour hand goes round the 12-number clock face twice — once from midday to midnight and once from midnight to midday — so 12 + 12 = 24, not 12. One lap alone is 12 hours; it takes two laps to make a day.
learnerActions: Move the hour hand slowly round an analogue clock from midday, naming the hours aloud as it passes the numbers.
When the hand returns to 12, pause and count: that first lap covered 12 hours (midday through to midnight).
Send the hand round a second time, now naming the night and morning hours, and track a day-strip that fills behind the clock — one half for the first lap, the second half for the second lap.
Write down the total: 12 + 12 = 24 hours in a whole day and night.
Line a 12-hour clock up beside a 24-hour clock so that, for example, 1pm matches 13:00, confirming the numbers 1-12 get used twice.
activities.title: The hour hand's double lap: why a day is 24 hours

feedback: If a learner says 90 minutes is 9 hours (or 0.9 of an hour), count minutes in fives to 60 on the number line so a full 60 closes into one hour before applying it to 90.
If they add times like 3:40 + 30 = 3:70, show that past 60 the minutes roll over into the next hour (3:40 + 30 = 4:10).
If they say half an hour is 50 minutes, count in fives to the halfway point and confirm it is 30, because half of 60 is 30, not half of 100.
Praise correct regrouping by asking them to explain WHY it is 60 and not 100.
activities.intendedInsight: Minutes regroup into hours at 60, not at 100: a full 60 minutes makes one hour, so 90 minutes is 1 hour 30 minutes — the grouping is felt by counting and overflowing, not just recited.
learnerActions: Count minutes in fives around a clock face or along a number line marked in minutes, saying 5, 10, 15 … up to 60.
Notice that it takes exactly 60 minutes for the minute hand to complete one full lap (twelve jumps of 5), so 60 minutes close into 1 hour.
Contrast this with money/base-10 out loud: an hour is 60 minutes, NOT 100 — time does not group in tens and hundreds.
Fill an 'hour container' that only closes at 60: pour in 90 minutes and watch it overflow into one full hour (60) with 30 left over.
Record the result: 90 minutes = 1 hour 30 minutes, because 90 = 60 + 30.
activities.title: Closing the hour at 60: the non-decimal grouping

feedback: Correct answer, no reason: ask them to show where the 60 or the double sweep is doing the work.
For the day item, a 12-hour answer signals the double-sweep misconception — return to tracking the hour hand round twice.
For the 90-minute item, a 9-hour or 0.9 answer signals missing 60-regrouping — return to counting minutes in fives to 60.
Mark as secure only when the learner states the fact AND explains it AND applies it to a new duration.
activities.intendedInsight: The time-unit facts are tools to be used: a learner who understands them can convert 90 minutes to 1 hour 30 and explain 24 hours as two 12-hour sweeps, transferring the reasoning to fresh problems.
learnerActions: Solve a duration problem such as: 'A cartoon lasts 90 minutes. How many hours and minutes is that, and how do you know?' and state the answer as 1 hour 30 minutes.
Answer a day question with reasoning: 'How many hours are in one whole day and night, and why — when the clock only shows 1 to 12?'
Decide which unit is larger, a minute or an hour, and justify it.
Explain each answer in words, not just give the number, so the reasoning is visible.
activities.title: Apply the facts: simple duration problems
